13-001.r: Father of computers → Charles Babbage: his Analytical Engine (1837; 1834 per NCERT) was the first general-purpose computer concept, with ALU and memory; never built in his lifetime.

13-004.r: Colossus, electronic digital computer for British code-breakers (1943–1945), was designed by Tommy Flowers; book's answer Alan M. Turing (contributed, not directly involved).

13-006.r: First digital computer built with IC chips → IBM System/360, a mainframe developed in 1964.

13-007.r: Main circuit board of a computer → motherboard; its chipset manages data flow between processor, memory and peripherals.

13-008.r: Pen drive (USB flash drive) → removable, portable secondary storage unit; it replaced floppy drives.

13-009.r: Mouse → input device (invented by Douglas Engelbart, 1963); it controls a pointer in a graphical user interface. Not an output device.

13-011.r: Monitor, printer, plotter → output devices; touch screen → both input (touch panel) and output (display).
13-011.c: The book gives no single answer (*): every option works as an output device, the touch screen being both input and output.

13-012.r: Only output devices: plotter, printer, monitor; scanner, keyboard, mouse, joystick and light pen are input devices.

13-013.r: Digital camera → input device; drum pen plotter, CRT monitor and earphones → output devices.

13-014.r: Only input devices: mouse, keyboard, scanner (also microphone, joystick, light pen); printer, projector, monitor, speaker, plotter are output.

13-015.r: Most common input devices → keyboard (text entry) and mouse (pointing); book answers keyboard, and mouse in a variant.

13-017.r: First mouse (Douglas Engelbart, built 1964) had a wooden body with two metal wheels; shown publicly in 1968.

13-018.r: Double-clicking the mouse sends the command to the CPU.

13-019.r: Keyboard cable plugs into a USB (Universal Serial Bus) port, which connects and powers peripherals.

13-020.r: Computer stores and analyses data, keeps it secure (passwords) and can be attacked by viruses → book: all four.

13-021.r: E-waste from old computers → beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead; not heptachlor (an insecticide) or plutonium (radioactive).

13-022.r: 'Network of networks' → Internet: a global network of computers linked by the TCP/IP protocol suite.

13-024.r: DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) → internet connection over telephone lines.

13-025.r: Slowest internet connection → dial-up (up to 56 Kbps); cable modem 512 kbps to 20 Mbps; leased lines give businesses fast access 24 hours a day.
13-025.c: One line in the book says dial-up speed is 'the same as a cable modem'; that contradicts its own point that dial-up is the slowest.

13-026.r: First page of a website (first shown by the browser) → home page; it leads to the site's other pages.

13-028.r: Common network topologies → star, bus, ring, tree, mesh, hybrid; grid is not a common topology.

13-029.r: Internet uses tree topology (book): a hybrid of bus and star; the internet is the largest hybrid topology.

13-030.r: Internet works on packet switching: data is split into blocks (packets) sent over the network.

13-031.r: Domain Name System (DNS) → database of host names and addresses; translates domain names into IP addresses.

13-032.r: IPv6 → 128-bit addresses (made by IETF to end IPv4 address exhaustion); IPv4 uses 32-bit; IPv6 became an Internet Standard on 14 July 2017.

13-033.r: Bluetooth → wireless communication between devices using radio waves; developed in 1994 by Jaap Haartsen.

13-034.r: Bluetooth → 2.4 GHz band (short range); Wi-Fi → 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz bands.
13-034.h: Wi-Fi has two lanes (2.4 and 5 GHz); Bluetooth has one (2.4 GHz).

13-036.r: First Indian railway station with Google's free public Wi-Fi → Mumbai Central (January 2016), under the 12 September 2015 Railways–Google tie-up for 400 stations.

13-037.r: Li-Fi → uses light waves (not radio) for wireless high-speed data; several times faster than Wi-Fi → both correct.

13-038.r: Li-Fi (Light Fidelity; Harald Hass, 2011): tested in India on 29 January 2018 by the IT Ministry (not I&B) with IIT Madras; uses lights, not optical fibre.

13-039.r: Internet → the largest network linking and storing information among countries through satellites and cables.

13-040.r: VPN (Virtual Private Network) → extends a private network across a public network (internet), letting users securely reach their organisation's network.

13-041.r: Portal → website offering many services: search, e-mail, news, stock prices, weather, sports, entertainment.

13-042.r: Talaash → C-DAC's multimedia internet portal and Devanagari OCR (optical character recognition) software.

13-043.r: NAYAN → C-DAC software to guard against cyber attacks and data theft.

13-044.r: PARAM supercomputers → designed and assembled by C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing), Pune.
13-044.h: PARAM from Pune: both start with P.

13-045.r: First indigenous Indian supercomputer → PARAM-8000, unveiled by C-DAC in 1991.

13-047.r: Father of Indian supercomputer → Vijay Bhatkar (PARAM-8000, unveiled 1991).

13-048.r: Anupam → BARC's supercomputer project (from 1991, parallel processing); the first was Anupam 860/4.

13-049.r: Supercomputer word length → up to 64 bits; personal computer generally 32 bits.

13-050.r: Supercomputer → the largest, fastest and costliest type of computer.

13-051.r: In 1996 the fastest computer (ASCI Red) did over 1 Teraflop/s, a trillion operations per second (option c); El Capitan (US) now does 1809 Petaflop/s (November 2025).

13-052.r: Fastest computer: IBM Roadrunner (USA) in 2008, when asked; Tianhe-1A (China) topped later; El Capitan (USA) per the November 2025 Top 500 list.
13-052.c: No option is right. When asked (2008) the fastest computer was IBM's Roadrunner (USA); Tianhe-1A, which the book names, reached the top only later. El Capitan led the November 2025 list.

13-053.r: 'Magic Cube' supercomputer → China; built to model Earth's future climate and biological systems.

13-054.r: India's fastest supercomputer on 31 March 2018 → Pratyush ('sun'; IITM Pune, January 2018; monsoon and weather forecasts); now fifth in India.

13-055.r: PARAM Kamrupa supercomputer → IIT Guwahati, inaugurated by President Droupadi Murmu on 13 October 2022 (838 TFLOPS, National Supercomputing Mission).

13-056.r: Smallest, fastest brain-like computer → quantum computer, based on qubits that can give many possible answers to one question.

13-057.r: Y2K (Year 2000 / Millennium bug) → computer coding problem when the year's last two digits became zero at the start of 2000; K = thousand.

13-059.r: Not matched: PARAM 10,000 is a C-DAC supercomputer, not a missile. Y2K → computer; arthritis → uric acid; noise pollution → decibel.

13-060.r: W.L.L. → Wireless in Local Loop: BSNL's communication service for rural areas.

13-061.r: Most widely used computers → microcomputers (desktops, laptops, tablets, smartphones, PDAs).

13-062.r: Digital watch → embedded computer: a dedicated computer inside a larger device (also MP3 players, traffic lights, MRI).

13-063.r: Laser printers (and CD/DVD players) → semiconductor laser; excimer → eye surgery, microelectronics; gas laser → holograms, barcodes; dye laser → spectroscopy.

13-064.r: Desktop printing (desktop publishing, DTP) → laser printer.

13-065.r: Daisy wheel printer → impact printer (David S. Lee, Diablo Data Systems, 1969); dot matrix printers are also impact printers.

13-066.r: WWW → World Wide Web: invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, opened to public in 1991; works on HTTP.

13-070.r: WWW is a hypermedia system because it links to other computer resources: interlinked hypertext documents reached through hyperlinks.

13-072.r: W3C → World Wide Web Consortium, the main web standards body, founded in 1994 by Tim Berners-Lee.

13-073.r: Computerisation of a system needs will, financial resources, trained manpower and modern infrastructure → all four (book).

13-074.r: Book: cyberspace, upload and modem are infotech terms; optical storage belongs to computer engineering.

13-075.r: Pinaka is not an infotech term: it is DRDO's multiple rocket launcher for the Indian Army; login, modem and password are.

13-076.r: Protocol, login and Archie (search program for anonymous FTP servers) → all are infotech terms.

13-077.r: Set of rules governing data communication → protocol (an agreement between communicating devices).

13-078.r: Protocol suite for all internet transmissions → TCP/IP: TCP makes and checks packets; IP addresses each packet to its place.

13-079.r: IP addresses work at the network layer (layer 3) of the OSI model (internet layer of TCP/IP); a logical address given by administrator or ISP.

13-080.r: OSI model (1984) has seven layers: physical (1), data link (2), network (3) → data link layer lies between physical and network.

13-081.r: IoT layers: perception (sensing), transport, network (connections, routing), application; book's answer for wireless connection: network layer.

13-082.r: Book: 'network server' is not a type of server; file, print, application, web, proxy, mail and database servers are.

13-085.r: 'Spam' relates to computers: flooding the internet with copies of the same message, mostly commercial advertising.

13-086.r: Repeatedly sending the same e-mail to one address to overflow the mailbox → e-mail bombing.

13-087.r: DuckDuckGo → search engine that does not collect user information.

13-088.r: Orkut → a (now closed) social networking site, not a search engine; Google, Altavista and ScienceDirect are search engines.

13-089.r: Baidu → Chinese search engine (websites, audio files, images).

13-090.r: Bing → web search engine of Microsoft, launched in 2009.

13-091.r: Kurrently → free social-media search engine giving real-time results from Twitter, Facebook etc.

13-093.r: Yahoo is a search engine, not a web browser; Internet Explorer (now Edge), Mozilla Firefox and Google Chrome are browsers.
13-093.t: Don't confuse a browser (Chrome, Firefox) with a search engine (Yahoo).

13-094.r: Google's web browser → Chrome (freeware, first released 2008).
